prompt: A nursery has two groups of the same crop species: cuttings from one parent, and seedlings from several crosses. A disease arrives. Assuming some inherited combinations reduce susceptibility, which group is more likely to contain genetic differences in response? Why can neither group be promised complete survival? Pause here to explain your reasoning.
feedback: The seedlings from several crosses are more likely to contain different inherited allele combinations. Under the stated assumption, some combinations may reduce susceptibility. The cuttings usually retain a much narrower set of combinations, so a shared susceptibility can put many at risk. Neither group has guaranteed survival. Relevant variants might be absent from particular offspring, and exposure and conditions still matter. Mutation can also introduce differences within a clonal group. The useful answer connects inheritance to risk, then bounds the prediction.
